newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Dogged Australian dlr recoups offshore losses.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Dogged Australian dlr recoups offshore losses.

text.p: The Australian dollar regained offshore losses and the 79 cent level in a dogged rally Tuesday but was well adrift on the yen and short of safe territory.
An eventful session saw it start at one-month lows as U.S. banks sold heavily, but bids from local exporters and an upbeat report on A$ bonds from a U.S. investment bank stopped the rot.
AUD/yen buying from Tokyo and talk of a revival in samurai issues also helped, but the support evaporated when comments from various Japanese ministers sent US$/yen diving.
A soft set of domestic retail data were largely lost in the tumult, but served to keep rate cut speculation alive.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local currency had barged back to US$0.7904/09 from an early US$0.7885/90 and a US$0.7870 low offshore, to be steady on Monday's late US$0.7903/08.
Traders said the offshore pressure had come largely from U.S. speculators looking to break key support at US$0.7850 and trigger stop loss selling.

Local corporates and funds were keen to buy for forex cover, however, and sentiment was further bolstered by talk a U.S. investment bank had advised clients to switch to Australian bonds from Canadian, although dealers emphasised the bank had not recommended going long of the dollar itself.
The local unit fared less well against the yen to finish at 91.05/15 yen from 92.15/25 late here Monday. In trade weighted terms it dipped to 58.8 from 59.1.
A seesaw session saw it rally at first on modest buying out of Tokyo only to come unstuck as a parade of top Japanese officials tried to talk down US$/yen.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka summed up the message by saying an excessively weak yen was bad for the economy and Japan would act against excessive dollar moves.
That saw the U.S. dollar flee to 115.20/25 yen from an early 115.80/85 and 116.40/45 late Monday.

Nevertheless, some of the impact was softened when the Tokyo stock market tumbled almost 550 points to breach the 19,000 support level. This was the latest episode in a dramatic slide which has seen the Nikkei lose 10 percent since early December and provided further reassurance that Japanese rates would be staying at record lows for some months to come.

That was welcome news to A$ bulls who have been worried that falling rates here would turn Japanese retail investors away from A$ denominated paper. Indeed, traders said there was talk a couple of smallish yen/A$ dual currency samurais bonds were due to be launched this week after almost a month of no issues.

But the risk of another domestic easing still lay ahead and today's data did nothing to lessen the chance with retail sales rising only a modest 0.7 percent in November and October's gain revised down to 1.2 percent from 1.4 percent.

The gains were not enough to compensate for September's 3.7 percent plunge and analysts said it looked like real retail sales were unlikely to make any contribution to GDP growth for Q4 and could even detract from growth unless the Christmas season proved strong.
This looked unlikely as two store chains today announced dissapointing sales and big profit downgrades.
Figures for building approvals were somewhat more upbeat as the fall of 1.6 percent reported for November barely dented the hefty 12.8 percent jump seen in October.

Approvals for the important private housing sector actually rose 4.7 percent and the value of non-residential building continued its spectacular upward run with a 58 percent rise to A$1.68 billion thanks to the inclusion of the Sydney Olympic Stadium.
The only other domestic data this week are November job vacancies on Thursday and private sector credit.
